questions.q: What is the single most important test an alert must pass before paging a human?
options: Is the metric collected every 10 seconds?
Is there something the person paged can actually do right now?
Does the alert have a colorful dashboard?
Is the threshold a round number?
questions.explain: An alert that pages someone with no actionable response available just trains people to ignore pages — actionability is the core test.

questions.q: Why is symptom-based alerting generally preferred over cause-based alerting for paging?
options: Cause-based alerts are always wrong
Symptom-based alerts fire on user-visible impact, catching problems regardless of their internal cause, and avoid paging for conditions that aren't actually hurting users
Symptom-based alerts don't require any metrics
Cause-based alerts can only be set up in Prometheus
questions.explain: High CPU alone doesn't always hurt users, and some user-impacting problems don't show up as high CPU — symptom-based alerting (e.g. checkout success rate) catches real impact either way.

questions.q: What does 'burn-rate alerting' tie the alert threshold to?
options: The age of the service
An arbitrary round number chosen once by a developer
How fast the error budget (derived from the SLO) is being consumed
The number of log lines produced per second
questions.explain: Burn-rate alerting ties thresholds directly to the SLO math — e.g. alerting when the error budget would be exhausted within a specific time window at the current failure rate.

questions.q: According to this lesson's alerting hierarchy, what should happen before a human is paged?
options: Nothing — humans should always be paged first for speed
The system should attempt cheaper automated responses first, like auto-remediation or self-healing
The alert should be deleted
The SLO should be lowered
questions.explain: The lesson recommends trying auto-remediation (restart, scale up, self-heal) before paging a human, reserving human paging for when those options are exhausted or human judgment is required.

questions.q: Northbridge pages an on-call engineer because disk usage is at 60% with no immediate action available. What does this lesson say about that alert?
options: It's a good alert because disk usage is important
It's a bad alert — it should likely be a non-urgent ticket or dashboard item, not a page, since there's nothing actionable to do right now
It should page two engineers instead of one
It should be escalated to a SEV1 immediately
questions.explain: An alert that pages someone with no actionable response fails the actionable test and shouldn't exist as a page — a dashboard or low-urgency ticket is more appropriate.
